title: Non-disruptive DR Drills for Oracle Databases Using Everpure ActiveDR — Part 2 of 4
summary: See how in a few simple steps you can complete the necessary configuration at the Non-disruptive DR site to open a database on demand.
body_markdown:
This is part two of a four-part series on using Everpure ActiveDR to protect, test, and fail over Oracle databases without taking production offline.


- [Part 1: Configure Everpure ActiveDR and protect your database volumes](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-everpure-activedr/)
- Part 2: Access the database volumes at the DR site and open the database (this post)
- [Part 3: Run non-disruptive DR drills with simple scripting](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-everpure-activedr-part-3-of-4/)
- [Part 4: Controlled and emergency failovers and failbacks](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-everpure-activedr-part-4-of-4/)


In part 1, we configured Everpure ActiveDR and protected an Oracle database’s volumes with a pod replicated to the DR site.


The raw volumes are safe at the DR site, but they’re not useful yet — nothing can read them until an Oracle database is configured to open them. That’s what this part covers: a one-time setup that brings an Oracle database online at the DR site using the replicated volumes.


### Connect the Replicated Volumes


The DR hosts, fbperf1 and fbperf2, are already connected to the DR array with a host group configured for both. First, connect the newly replicated volumes to that host group:


```text
everpurehgroup connect --vol Oracle-DR::oracle-acrac-actdrdbs-CONTROL_REDO fbperf
everpurehgroup connect --vol Oracle-DR::oracle-acrac-actdrdbs-DATA fbperf
everpurehgroup connect --vol Oracle-DR::oracle-acrac-actdrdbs-FRA fbperf
```


The volumes typically appear in /dev/mapper immediately. If they don’t, rescan the host bus adapters on each node:


```text
for f in /sys/class/scsi_host/host?/scan
do
echo "scanning $f" ; echo "- - -" > $f
done
```


For each volume, match its serial number (ls -l /dev/mapper) against the serial shown in the array console, and add friendly device names to /etc/multipath.conf on all RAC nodes:


This example matches serial 21f018170267441100011491, which gives us:


```text
multipath {
wwid 3624a937021f018170267441100011491
alias dg_acrac_actdrdbs_control_redo
}
multipath {
wwid 3624a937021f01817026744110001148f
alias dg_acrac_actdrdbs_data
}
multipath {
wwid 3624a937021f018170267441100011490
alias dg_acrac_actdrdbs_fra
}
```


Reload multipath as root (multipath -r). The friendly names are now visible in /dev/mapper:


```text
ls -l /dev/mapper | grep actdrdbs


lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 8 May 5 17:30 dg_acrac_actdrdbs_control_redo -> ../dm-45


lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 8 May 5 17:30 dg_acrac_actdrdbs_data -> ../dm-46


lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 8 May 5 17:29 dg_acrac_actdrdbs_fra -> ../dm-44
```


This example uses Oracle ASMLib 3.1 to prepare devices for ASM in a multipathed environment. Because Oracle ASM filtering is disabled on Linux kernel 5.14 and later, ASMFD users should migrate to ASMLib 3.1 where applicable.


Since the devices are multipathed, first make sure ASMLib scans the /dev/mapper device-mapper names rather than the underlying /dev/sd* paths. Edit /etc/sysconfig/oracleasm on each node and set:


```text
ORACLEASM_SCANORDER="dm"
ORACLEASM_SCANEXCLUDE="sd"
```


Then scan for disks so ASMLib can discover them on all nodes:


```text
/usr/sbin/oracleasm scandisks


/usr/sbin/oracleasm listdisks


ADR_CONTROL_REDO


ADR_DATA


ADR_FRA
```


Keep in mind that oracleasm listdisks shows ASMLib disk names (labels), not device paths — if you want to show the path-to-label mapping too, oracleasm querydisk -d <label> gives that.


After the scan, the disk labels already appear — they were written into the ASMLib disk headers at the production site (via oracleasm createdisk) and replicated across to DR along with the data.


### Promote the DR Pod and Mount the Diskgroups


To mount the disk groups and register the new database instance with Oracle Clusterware, the Oracle-DR pod must be temporarily promoted to read/write. Promotion creates a writable DR point-in-time snapshot while preserving the original state in the background, so the pod can later be demoted and rolled back cleanly. During that window, writes coming from production are queued rather than applied immediately to the DR volumes, and they are replayed only after the pod is demoted again once DR-site configuration is complete. This approach lets you run DR drills without disrupting the production database or affecting its performance.


As the grid user, mount the diskgroups on all RAC nodes:


```text
echo "alter diskgroup ADR_CONTROL_REDO mount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm


echo "alter diskgroup ADR_DATA mount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm


echo "alter diskgroup ADR_FRA mount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm
```


### Register the database with Clusterware


Recreate the directory structure from the production hosts at the DR site before adding it to the Clusterware configuration. As the Oracle user, on all RAC nodes:


```text
mkdir -p /u01/app/oracle/local/admin/ACTDRDBS/adump
mkdir -p /u01/app/oracle/local/diag/rdbms/actdrdbs/ACTDRDBS1/cdump
```


Pull the relevant configuration details from the production database:


```text
srvctl config database -d ACTDRDBS


Database unique name: ACTDRDBS


Database name: ACTDRDBS


Oracle home: /u01/app/oracle/product/db/12cR2


Oracle user: oracle


Spfile: +ADR_CONTROL_REDO/ACTDRDBS/PARAMETERFILE/spfile.270.1136027663


Password file: +ADR_CONTROL_REDO/ACTDRDBS/PASSWORD/pwdactdrdbs.256.1136027291


Domain: puresg.com


Start options: open


Stop options: immediate


Database role: PRIMARY


Management policy: AUTOMATIC


Disk Groups: ADR_FRA,ADR_CONTROL_REDO,ADR_DATA


Database instances: ACTDRDBS1,ACTDRDBS2


Configured nodes: acrac1,acrac2
```


Reuse several of these values for the DR-site configuration. The Oracle home path differs slightly at the DR site, reflected below. Note this uses role PRIMARY, since this database isn’t managed by Data Guard, and policy MANUAL, since the database can only start while its volumes are read/write — which only happens while the Oracle-DR pod is promoted — so we don’t want Clusterware attempting to start it automatically:


```text
srvctl add database \


-db ACTDRDBS \


-dbname ACTDRDBS \


-oraclehome /u01/app/oracle/product/23.26.1/dbhome_1 \


-spfile +ADR_CONTROL_REDO/ACTDRDBS/PARAMETERFILE/spfile.270.1136027663 \


-pwfile +ADR_CONTROL_REDO/ACTDRDBS/PASSWORD/pwdactdrdbs.256.1136027291 \


-startoption OPEN \


-stopoption IMMEDIATE \


-role PRIMARY \


-policy MANUAL \


-diskgroup ADR_FRA,ADR_CONTROL_REDO,ADR_DATA \


-dbtype RAC
```


Add the database to /etc/oratab on both nodes:


```text
vi /etc/oratab


ACTDRDBS1:/u01/app/oracle/product/23.26.1/dbhome_1:N


+ASM1:/u01/app/grid/product/23.26.1/grid:N


Start the database at the DR site:


srvctl start database -d ACTDRDBS


Then create a RAC service for client connections:


srvctl add service -db ACTDRDBS -service ACTDRDBS_DR -preferred "ACTDRDBS1,ACTDRDBS2"


srvctl start service -db ACTDRDBS -service ACTDRDBS_DR


An example TNS connect string for this service:


(DESCRIPTION=


(TRANSPORT_CONNECT_TIMEOUT=5) (RETRY_COUNT=6) (FAILOVER=ON)


(ADDRESS = (PROTOCOL = TCP) (HOST = fbperf-scan) (PORT = 1521))


(CONNECT_DATA= (SERVER = DEDICATED) (SERVICE_NAME = ACTDRDBS_DR.puresg.com))


)
```


### Return the pod to a demoted state


This one-time setup is done. Shut the database down, unmount the ASM diskgroups, and demote the Oracle-DR pod so replication can catch up and continue streaming production writes:


```text
srvctl stop database -d ACTDRDBS -o immediate
```


As the grid user:


```text
echo "alter diskgroup ADR_CONTROL_REDO dismount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm


echo "alter diskgroup ADR_DATA dismount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm


echo "alter diskgroup ADR_FRA dismount force;" | sqlplus -s / as sysasm
```


The production database is replicating, and the DR site is fully configured to open that database on demand, without ever touching production. Part 3 covers turning this into a simple, repeatable script for on-demand, non-disruptive DR drills.
